channel.title: One Author — Networking and Internet Architecture

item.title: An Improved $(1+2e)$-Approximation Algorithm for Metric Data Placement
item.description: We study the metric data placement problem with site-capacity constraints and fixed installation costs, aiming to minimize the total cost of placing data (resources) and accessing their nearest copies. We develop a deterministic polynomial-time approximation algorithm based on a natural linear programming relaxation of the problem. Starting from an optimal fractional solution, we construct multiscale metric-ball partitions independently for each resource and connect overlapping balls at consecutive levels to form a flow network. The resource layers are then coupled through shared site-capacity arcs, allowing us to obtain an integral placement by minimizing a surrogate cost over a single min-cost circulation. By optimizing the choice of ball radii, we establish an approximation factor of $1+2e\approx 6.44$. To our knowledge, this is the best approximation guarantee for the metric data placement problem since its introduction by Baev and Rajaraman in 2001.

item.title: Perception-Limited UAV Positioning: On the Reliability of Line-of-Sight Constraints in Sensing-Driven Aerial Networks
item.description: Unmanned Aerial Vehicles carrying access points or base stations are widely positioned so as to hold line-of-sight links with every ground user at once. The algorithms that do so are evaluated against obstacle information treated as exact, whether that information comes from a surveyed map or, more recently, from onboard vision. This paper analyses what becomes of that requirement when the obstacle information is estimated rather than given, and derives the detection accuracy it implicitly demands. Three results follow. The probability of satisfying the requirement decays geometrically with the number of users, so that a detector accurate enough for one user is not accurate enough for a network. Spatially correlated detection error raises that probability but concentrates failures into systematic blind spots. Relaxing the requirement from all users to ninety per cent of them widens the tolerable detection error by more than an order of magnitude, far beyond what any plausible improvement of the detector could deliver. item.title: Semantic-Aware Communications in Industrial IoT:What Can Be Tested Today, and What Is Missing?
item.description: Classical networks treat every bit as equally important, which wastes time and energy in factories and requires extra traffic engineering for critical traffic. Semantic communications send only what a task needs, but how can they be tested under realistic conditions? This paper examines what can be tested today in 6G industrial IoT, that is, networks of factory machines, robots, and sensors, and what is still missing. It introduces semantic importance, a score attached to each message that states how much the message matters, and uses it in a context-driven design to derive eight testing needs. Existing simulators, emulators, testbeds, codecs, and learning frameworks are assessed against these needs, which reveals five gaps. We propose a toolchain of four components built around the ns-3 simulator for simulated and emulated scenarios.

item.title: Advancements in Cloud-Native Systems: A Systematic Mapping Study of Reliability and Scalability across Cloud-Native, Edge-Native and AI-Enabled Systems
item.description: Cloud-native systems now extend to the network edge and host artificial-intelligence (AI) workloads, including AI agents, but evidence on their reliability and scalability is scattered and uneven. We report a PRISMA 2020 systematic mapping study with an evidence-graded synthesis. Five logged OpenAlex searches on 11 October 2026 covered cloud-native systems, edge AI, agentic AI for operations, reliability of agentic applications and physical AI; 189 records from an earlier exploratory search were added separately. After 301 duplicate removals and an automated peer-review venue rule, 4,611 records were screened against written criteria and a five-level relevance scale. The review includes 1,794 primary studies from 2017-2026 and 95 secondary studies, with every decision released in Dataset S1. Each primary study was assigned to a 13-category taxonomy and graded as simulation, prototype or testbed, production data, production deployment, or not determinable from the abstract. Of 1,003 studies with a determinable level, 66.2% used prototypes or testbeds, 18.0% simulations and 15.8% production data or deployments. A 93-study synthesis core, appraised from indexed abstracts, shows production deployments of cascading-failure prevention, trace- and graph-based root-cause analysis and predictive autoscaling, and production-trace evaluations of cold-start mitigation. Edge reliability and physical AI rely mainly on simulations and testbeds. AI-agent reliability uses tool-grounded diagnosis, explicit safety properties, trace-driven repair and workload-aware scheduling, while empirical studies show that agent frameworks remain fragile. Conclusions are limited to the documented corpus. The principal gaps are production evidence for edge-native systems, shared resilience benchmarks and dependable agentic operations.

item.title: From Radio Measurements to Sensing Services: A 3GPP Perspective on Multi-UAV Tracking with Networked ISAC
item.description: Integrated sensing and communication (ISAC) can turn radio measurements into networked sensing services, but accurate position estimates alone do not ensure useful tracking. Missed targets, late acquisition, track interruptions and aging observations also shape the information available to an application. This article examines tracking of noncooperative unmanned aerial vehicles (UAVs) from a Third Generation Partnership Project (3GPP) perspective. It connects sensing-service requirements and network architecture to three information interfaces: receiver search regions, measurement context and track validity. A five-UAV case study in a 3GPP urban scenario and a ray-traced San Francisco scene illustrates the tradeoff between target coverage and extra outputs, the distinction between acquisition and ongoing continuity, and the value of testing a static mission envelope before adding adaptation. An observation-age example explains how a state predicted to the present can still rely on old evidence. The resulting lessons are to align receiver search with requested coverage, preserve measurement time and uncertainty, and assess coverage, ambiguity and timeliness together. We conclude by pointing out fruitful avenues for further work in sensing design, calibration and service validation.

item.title: VLA Handover: Failure-Prediction-Based Switching from On-Robot to Server VLA Models
item.description: Large vision-language-action (VLA) models generalize well but are difficult to run in real time on a robot, and small VLAs that run there fail more often. Remote inference over beyond-5G and 6G networks lets a robot use a large VLA on a server, but querying the server for every action chunk limits the number of robots per server. We propose VLA handover: the robot runs a small VLA (S-VLA) and switches to a large VLA (L-VLA) on a server only when the S-VLA is likely to fail. We formulate the switching as minimizing the request cost under a required success probability and, since this problem cannot be solved directly, propose a heuristic framework that retrains neither VLA. In simulation with SmolVLA and $π_{0.5}$ on three of the four LIBERO suites, VLA handover raised the success rate by 11-22 percentage points over the S-VLA alone and sent 49-77% fewer requests than server-only control at a 2-4 percentage-point lower success rate, and its completion time grew less with the network latency.

item.title: Characterizing AI Service Traffic for 6G: An Open Testbed and Initial Results from 3GPP SA4
item.description: The design of sixth generation (6G) mobile systems requires measurements of artificial intelligence (AI) service traffic under controlled network conditions. The 3rd Generation Partnership Project (3GPP) Service and System Aspects Working Group 4 (SA4) documents such measurements in draft Technical Report 26.870. In this paper, we describe the open testbed used for the study and analyze the results recorded in version 0.6.2 and its companion workbook. The testbed combines network emulation, packet capture, application measurements, and scenario execution against hosted and self-hosted models. The reported uplink to downlink volume ratios span more than six orders of magnitude. A personal assistant agent has a ratio of 0.007 at its local control interface and 0.50 on its wide-area egress. Deterministic agent signaling follows the configured round-trip delay. In a tokenized video experiment with 125 questions per profile, the number of correct answers changes by at most three through 10% independent uplink loss. Larger losses reduce accuracy, but the available repetitions do not establish a tolerance threshold. We also analyze emulator behavior that affects the interpretation of the study. Per-packet jitter introduces reordering, correlated random-loss settings suppress rare loss events, and a Gilbert-Elliott parameter mapping changes the stationary loss rate. The results support characterization by scenario, measurement layer, and versioned network configuration.

item.title: Clear Human Web: Where a Person Vouches for Every Client
item.description: The web cannot tell whether a request comes from a person or from a program. Sites have checked the network address and puzzles in its place, and both have given way: automated traffic exceeds human traffic, and puzzles are solved for pay and by agents. This paper proposes the Clear Human Web, the part of the public web that sites open only to clients a person vouches for. A person's wallet presents their person identification data (PID) to one issuer, the only party that registers as a relying party, and receives a bounded number of blind-signed tokens, proofs of personhood that carry no attribute. The browser spends one token at each site that runs the gate, and the site learns that a valid token of a trusted issuer was spent, and nothing else. No field is added to the PID, no protocol is introduced, no site registers, and the publisher of a site holds the same proof as its readers. We define the Clear Human Web through five properties and seven adversaries, and state which properties the construction satisfies against each adversary. The identities a person can hold on one site in an epoch are bounded to k. The bound holds once the wallet limits a person to one pseudonym at the issuer. In the optimum k = 1, and a zero-knowledge proof of PID possession and a pseudonym per site replace the tokens.

item.title: Wireless Networks That See: Integrated Sensing and Communication in Complex Environments
item.description: The same radio interactions that complicate wireless communication can reveal what is happening around a network. Integrated sensing and communication (ISAC) turns these interactions into opportunities to observe unmanned aerial vehicles (UAVs), road vehicles, and industrial mobile robots. Yet a strong echo is not necessarily a reliable object observation: stationary background can conceal motion, reflections can create virtual objects, and one viewpoint can leave part of an object's motion unobserved. This tutorial explains how known cellular signals are used to estimate propagation, suppress stationary background, interpret reflected paths, and combine observations from different sites. UAV examples under a Third Generation Partnership Project (3GPP) stochastic channel model and ray tracing in a San Francisco urban scene illustrate the mechanisms through spatial layouts, channel profiles, and before/after range--Doppler maps. Local checks reduce false outputs, with some loss of detection. Cooperation improves position accuracy for UAVs detected by both a single site and cooperating sites. The examples show how signal resources, measurement reporting, and application needs shape sensing performance, providing practical guidance for sensing services in complex environments.

item.title: Bounded Retained History in a Proxy Flow Replay: A Mixed Predictive Pilot and an Allocation Study
item.description: We examine bounded retained history through a frozen predictive pilot and a subsequent allocation study on a curated UNSW-NB15 flow mirror. Both use an artificial release-order replay based on raw ltime ticks, with equal-tick records querying a shared prior-group state. In the pilot, the model with added retained relational features had lower reconnaissance recall than the current-flow-plus-counters baseline (43.66% versus 47.84%) and lower benign false-positive rate (3.63% versus 6.68%) at separately frozen operating thresholds, together with lower AUROC. This mixed result did not establish a predictive advantage. A development-only audit subsequently found that capacity eviction dominated expiration in the 256-record, 300-tick FIFO state, with a median completed record lifetime of 11 ticks. A protocol specified before its single execution, but after the pilot and post-hoc mechanism audit, compared five label-blind retention arms on the already-used development trace. Its primary equal-source endpoint averaged retained/reference ratios for service-expanded source out-degree and source-destination service diversity. Source-balanced retention at 256 records exceeded FIFO-256 by a pooled endpoint difference of 0.440738 and met the prespecified materiality and subblock rule. Crucially, the event-weighted ratios for both quantities decreased relative to FIFO-256: the result is specific to the equal-source weighting objective and does not establish uniformly improved retention. The study supplies neither evidence of detection improvement nor an explanation of the pilot result. Reused data, concentrated reconnaissance support, proxy timing, and the absence of a qualified independent corpus bound the interpretation.

item.title: When 200 OK Is Not an Answer: Silent Fetch Failures in Agentic Web Content Acquisition
item.description: Web agents and answer engines fetch pages at question time, and liveness checks of cited sources treat an HTTP 200 response as success. We measure how often that assumption fails and what it does to measurements built on fetched pages. We fetched 10,307 URLs in three days with a polite static client and a rendered browser client: pages from 1,507 sites in five strata, random non-existent paths on every site, and the 4,795 URLs cited by expert-verified claims in ExpertQA. We define a taxonomy of what a 200 response contains, label the static 200 responses automatically, and check the labels against 300 items reviewed by an LLM-based assistant; a human check of 60 of them retained every reviewed usability label after discussion. By the automatic labels, 20.9% of the pages that a static client receives with status 200 do not contain the page's main content: app shells, bot challenges, block pages, error and placeholder pages, and partial content. On the held-out test split, the reviewed sample lowers this estimate from 25.5% to 20.0%. 13.1% of the sites whose random-path probe was answered returned 200. The error propagates: for the cited sources, treating 200 as content overstates the share of claim-source pairs that can be checked against live content by 12.2 points and inflates the apparent silent citation-drift rate from 5.8% to 21.9%. Cheap heuristics catch most of it. Text length, probe comparison and redirect-to-root, combined and tuned on held-out sites, recover 86% of unusable reviewed responses at a false-alarm rate near 5%. Content-reading detectors perform comparably: the best, the text classifier, gains five to seven points of recall at more than twice the false-alarm rate. We argue that agents and their evaluations should report fetch outcomes explicitly instead of inferring them from the status line and will release the labelled data and code.

item.title: Adaptive Dynamic Security for Operational Technology Against AI-Powered Attacks
item.description: Operational technology now faces attackers whose tempo is set by AI. We present ADS-OT, an adaptive dynamic security framework modelling defensive posture as a partially observable decision problem. A reinforcement-learning policy adapts monitoring, access, deception, and segmentation under a safety-governance layer, reducing attack-path completion, detection, and containment versus static baselines.

item.title: Do Open-Source Video Ad Clients Follow VAST 4.3? An Empirical Study of Player Conformance
item.description: Context. Video ads reach streaming and connected-TV apps through VAST documents, and companies count ads from the HTTP requests the player's client library sends. A tracking error can leave playback intact and surface later as disagreeing counts. Objective. To measure how far open-source VAST clients meet the player duties of VAST 4.3, whether verdicts depend on the runtime, what generated inputs add, and when deviations were introduced. Method. A catalog of 108 requirements was extracted from the specification. Six open-source clients in eight configurations ran against 69 crafted test vectors and the IAB's sample tags, under Node.js and in five browsers on three engines, with every request recorded. Grids, fuzzing and a sweep over 36 releases extend the catalog; Google's closed IMA SDK is a comparison. Results. The open-source clients have 78 findings and 3 to 21 must-level deviations per configuration. None of the tested open-source clients that follow redirect (Wrapper) chains fills the required macros in a Wrapper's request; the archived IMA 3.794.0 configuration tested does. One library's timeout throws an exception no caller can catch, ending a Node.js process. In a pod (ads played back to back), one player credits a finishing ad's completion to the next ad, fixed in release 5.3.0. A library can conform under jsdom and deviate in every tested Chrome- and Safari-family browser. Conclusions. The tested clients diverge on the duties other companies use to count and diagnose ads. A shared conformance suite run in real browsers could expose most graded deviations; the harness and vectors are released.

item.title: Sample-and-Score: Surrogate-Guided Coordinated Spatial Reuse in IEEE 802.11 Networks
item.description: Coordinated spatial reuse (Co-SR) in IEEE 802.11bn increases area throughput through simultaneous transmissions, yet the combinatorial configuration space makes real-time optimization challenging. We propose a sample-and-score approach: draw random Co-SR configurations, score each with a surrogate model, and select the best. The surrogate is trained offline and deployed without online fine-tuning or sequential exploration, yet performs close to multi-armed bandit and heuristic baselines that need multiple interaction steps or extensive measurements. On unseen topologies with 2-16 access points, it recovers 52-77% of a perfect surrogate's throughput. A perfect sample-and-score approach reaches 95% of the upper bound throughput with 8192 candidates.

item.title: Making the Telemetry Pipeline Measurable: An Edge IoT Testbed and Dataset for End-to-End Latency, Provenance, and Energy-Aware Benchmarking
item.description: Edge-centric IoT systems are increasingly evaluated through sensor values or platform features, yet the telemetry pipeline itself, the sequence of sensing, serialization, message mediation, ingestion, and persistence, is rarely released as a measurable object. This limits reproducible benchmarking of timeliness, provenance, and operational cost, especially in early-stage IoT design where real deployments and high-quality open data are often unavailable. I present a measurement-first edge IoT testbed and dataset that elevate timeliness, provenance, and energy to first-class telemetry dimensions. The testbed operationalizes a role-based event-driven architecture with explicit Source-Broker-Aggregator responsibilities and a schema-governed TelemetryMessage envelope (Avro) that embeds correlation identifiers and a uniform, cross-role vocabulary of stage-level timestamps. To trace mediation effects, I extend an MQTT broker (Eclipse Mosquitto) with a plugin that annotates messages with high-precision ingress/egress timestamps. I release the dataset in a dual representation: (i) replayable raw events as compressed Avro streams and (ii) analysis-ready long-format Parquet tables partitioned for efficient query and benchmarking, generated by a deterministic raw-to-tabular transformation pipeline. The contribution is an integrated engineering artifact and dataset built from established components. The demonstration describes one deployment through latency summaries, measurement-context distributions, and energy aggregates; it does not establish a new attribution method or a controlled performance benchmark. By co-releasing heterogeneous telemetry with pipeline timing and energy signals in both replayable and queryable forms, the artifact provides a basis for reproducible exploratory analysis and subsequent benchmarking studies.

item.title: Who Patches the Lightning Network? Evidence from Release Lines in Gossip, 2023-2026
item.description: Every implementation of Bitcoin's Lightning payment network disclosed security vulnerabilities in 2026, and every advisory told operators to upgrade. Whether they do has never been measured, because Lightning gossip carries no software version. Matching the feature bits a node announces against the source of every LND, Core Lightning, Eclair and LDK release, we show that gossip reveals a node's release line after all. Where Core Lightning nodes state their version, the inferred line is exact for 132 of 136 node-line pairs. Across 814 daily snapshots of the public graph from 2023 to 2026, the network patches on release and platform schedules, not on disclosures. Half of LND nodes upgrade within 88 days of a release; small nodes and those that skipped releases lag far behind. The three largest upgrade waves came about a day after the Umbrel app store shipped a new LND version. Since June 2025, 17% of LND upgrades came in the 48 hours after a platform release, windows that cover 4.4% of the time. Disclosures, a median 256 days after the fix, moved few operators: of 12 we can test, only Core Lightning's of July 2026 sped up upgrades, and only among nodes one release line behind. Its later call to restart offline was followed mostly by nodes already patched. Two months after Lightning Labs' August 2026 batch, 71% of the LND nodes exposed at disclosure still ran an affected release. For maintainers, the lever on the nodes that lag is the platforms that package their releases.

item.title: VX-One: Typed, Calibrated Decision Heads for Real-Time Perimeter Triage - An empirical study of unknown-attack honesty, cascade gray zones, and calibration under drift
item.description: Perimeter triage faces a latency/semantics trade-off: signature engines are fast and format-safe but blind to unseen attacks, while generative models are semantic but slow and produce unparseable output. In late 2026 a class of commercial System One decision models (TypeSafe Jev; Microsoft-Decision-1) began selling typed decision primitives - binary gates, closed-set choices, ordinal scores - as product APIs, with no academic treatment. We present VX-One: a small multi-head network (100K-10M parameters) whose outputs are these primitives - a calibrated gate, a choice over a closed candidate set that always includes an explicit unknown option, and an ordinal score, trained multi-task, temperature-calibrated per head (~0.7-1.7 ms p50 on CPU). We evaluate it on UNSW-NB15, CIC-IDS2017, EMBER2024 against calibrated XGBoost, Random-Forest, MLP, Kitsune, and measure a two-phase cascade (Suricata with 52,674 Emerging-Threats rules -> VX-One) over five days of CIC-IDS2017. Findings: (i) VX-One wins detection (AUROC/FPR@95%TPR) on UNSW-NB15 and under temporal drift on CIC-IDS2017 (0.711 vs 0.637), but XGBoost wins multi-class attribution on all three benchmarks; (ii) leave-one-family-out gate detects never-seen families on 9/9 UNSW folds yet drops below chance on CIC recon family, and abstention threshold transfers poorly across benchmarks; (iii) on payload-less reconstructions signature engines resolve ~0.1% of flows - gray zone ~99.9% of traffic, recovered by Phase 2 (combined recall >=0.978); (iv) calibration collapses under temporal drift (ECE 0.04->0.40) for every method while ranking partially survives. We provide a measured account of where typed calibrated decisions help perimeter triage, and where they fail.

item.title: Agent AI Zarządzający Siecią Open RAN Zorientowana na Użytkownika
item.description: Jednym z najważniejszych wyzwań związanych z implementacją sieci Open RAN o architekturze zorientowanej na użytkownika jest odpowiednie formowanie tzw. klastrów obsługujących. Problem ten może być efektywnie rozwiązany za pomocą zaproponowanego Agenta AI bazującego na modelu językowym. Wyniki symulacji pokazały, że zaproponowane rozwiązanie pozwala na ponad 2-krotne zwiększenie mediany rozkładu przepływności użytkowników względem standardowej architektury zorientowanej na sieć.

item.title: Joint Freshness and Deadline Feasibility in Store-and-Forward Satellite IoT Networks
item.description: 3GPP Release 19 supports store-and-forward satel- lite access, where traffic accumulated during feeder-link outages must be forwarded through finite, geometry-limited windows. Static priority levels offer little discrimination among large backlogs and ignore the decay in packet value. We formulate QoS feasibility for status updates, measured by destination freshness, and deadline-constrained event reports over periodic two-hop contacts with finite onboard storage. For general calendars, we derive ordering-sensitive miss, cohort-capacity, delivery-rate, and freshness bounds, including an exact status-only characterization. For single status flow and single event class sharing a contact pair per period, a finite-state program gives exact joint feasibility for arbitrary integer age thresholds. Numerical results quantify tradeoffs among load, capacity, deadline, and freshness tolerance.

item.title: Semantic Communications: Principles, Architectures and Applications
item.description: Conventional communication systems are designed to transmit data reliably, focusing on metrics such as bit error rate, throughput, and channel capacity. However, these traditional measures do not evaluate whether the received information is actually useful for a specific downstream task. To address this limitation, semantic communication has emerged as a promising paradigm that prioritizes the meaning, context, and task relevance of transmitted information rather than raw bit level reconstruction. This paper presents a comprehensive review of the theoretical foundations, system architectures, learning techniques, and evaluation practices in semantic communications. We classify existing state-of-the-art algorithms ranging from deep joint source-channel coding (Deep JSCC) and task-oriented feature transmission to generative diffusion models and contrast their operational trade offs against conventional baselines. Furthermore, we examine key application domains, including remote sensing, autonomous vehicles, and healthcare IoT, while addressing open challenges in security, privacy, robustness, and standardized evaluation.

item.title: Connection Escrow: Holding AI-Agent Pod Egress in the Kernel Until an Isolated Verifier Rules
item.description: AI agents in containers act by opening network connections, and the text that drives them can be hostile. Controls placed between the agent and its tools are bypassed by a child process or a direct socket, and their approval is not tied to the connection the kernel later opens. We present connection escrow: every outbound TCP connection from a supervised pod is parked inside the kernel's connect() path, before any packet exists, by a 98-instruction eBPF program on the pod's cgroup. A node interceptor attributes the held socket to its kernel socket cookie, process, executable digest, cgroup and pod identity, parks the first bytes the agent writes, and asks a verifier in a separate container with its own key. The connection is released only on a signed verdict naming that one socket cookie and destination, unexpired and unused; no verdict by the deadline resets it, and a late approval is refused. The agent is unmodified. A 36-check adversarial suite with real cgroups passes on the eBPF hold point (33 of the checks also apply, and pass, on an iptables hold point): refused connections never reach the destination; forged, rebound, replayed, expired and late verdicts are refused; the agent's attempt to reach the verifier is itself escrowed; child-process and renamed-binary bypasses fail; UDP is pinned to the resolver. On a Kubernetes cluster, unmodified pods are held per connection and attributed to their SPIFFE identity, a raw socket that bypasses a sidecar proxy is held, and 600 connections from six pods are gated. The hold adds 4.5 ms median per released connection, of which 24 us is policy. Finally, we gate on request content without terminating TLS: an eBPF uprobe reads the plaintext at the agent's TLS-library boundary (shared OpenSSL, static OpenSSL, Go crypto/tls), a model scores it, and the connection is held on that verdict while TLS stays end-to-end and the enforcer holds no key.

item.title: Off-Tree Forwarding for Accelerating Broadcasts from Arbitrary Sources in Plumtree
item.description: Overlay broadcast is fundamental to large-scale distributed systems, enabling messages to be disseminated to all participants. Plumtree is a well-established protocol that embeds a spanning tree in a gossip overlay: payloads are disseminated along tree links, while non-tree links support recovery and optimization. However, because the tree is constructed from the first broadcast, it is optimized for the initial source and can introduce long detours for broadcasts originating at other nodes, particularly leaf nodes. To address this limitation, we propose probabilistic exuding, an off-tree forwarding mechanism in which nodes near the source additionally forward payloads over their non-tree links with a specified probability. Exuded messages use a dedicated message type and do not participate in tree construction or repair, leaving the shared tree unchanged. Simulations on a 1000-node random regular overlay show that, for randomly selected sources and a representative parameter setting, the proposed method reduces the 95th-percentile delivery latency by approximately 40% relative to Plumtree. This closes approximately 92% of the latency gap between Plumtree and flooding while sending only about 58% as many payload messages as flooding. In contrast, Plumtree's own link optimization and shorter repair timeouts, which also exploit non-tree links, rewire the shared tree and increase latency as broadcast sources change; the latency of exuding is nearly unaffected.

item.title: From Trust Scores to Driver Decisions: An Abstaining Evidential Decision Layer for Event Validation in VANETs
item.description: Trust management in vehicular ad hoc networks is highly active, yet the decision that a driver needs, whether a reported event is real, has received far less attention; the schemes that make it force every decision into two outcomes, even on thin or conflicting evidence. This paper presents CREST, a vehicle-side event-decision framework that can withhold a decision its evidence does not support. Each vehicle weights the reports it holds by the trust, proximity and freshness of their senders, fuses them with Yager's rule, and decides only when the fused margin reaches an abstention threshold. Abstention is a waiting state: a vehicle still unsure at the event is resolved by an explicit application policy, which makes the trade-off between missed hazards and unnecessary detours visible. CREST requires only a scalar trust per reporter and is built here on an evidential trust model whose consensus and revocation steps are updated to support the decision layer. A single report is shown to change the decision margin by at most its weight, which bounds the influence of an attacker coalition by its trust. In a pre-registered simulation study with fourteen attacks, including position spoofing and trust-gated camouflage, and with all unspecified parameters of all systems tuned by the same procedure, CREST reduces the decision error of two published trust-based dissemination systems from 0.162 and 0.106 to 0.051. With the best-guess policy it also lowers both missed and unnecessary reroutes and outperforms the forced binary rule on both error types in every cell.

item.title: Retrospective Evaluation of Bluetooth RSSI Fingerprinting for Bin Localization on an Industrial Shop Floor
item.description: This paper evaluates an archival Bluetooth Low Energy received signal strength indicator (RSSI) dataset collected for bin localization on an industrial shop floor. The installation used 24 fixed relays positioned on walls and Bluetooth beacons attached to bins, with each relay applying a Kalman filter to its own readings in firmware before publishing them. The primary survey produced 19,034 usable two-minute fingerprint samples across 90 known positions, with 23 relay measurements available as model features. We compare calibrated path-loss multilateration with two radio-map estimators: distance-weighted $k$-nearest neighbours and Random Forest regression. A random 70/30 row split measures recognition at surveyed positions, while a coordinate-grouped split reserves 27 entire positions for testing and measures interpolation to unseen positions. Random Forest achieved a median error of 0.66~m for surveyed positions, with 77.9% of estimates within 3~m and 96.3% within 10~m. For unseen positions, median error increased to 9.42~m and 55.5% of estimates were within 10~m. Path-loss multilateration produced a 19.41~m median error on unseen positions, close to the 19.62~m mean-position baseline. The results support RSSI fingerprinting for a fixed inventory of surveyed bin positions, but not precise continuous localization between survey points. Git history dates the original implementation to September 7, 2019. The evaluation code in this paper was written in October 2026 and is reported separately from the seven-year-old prototype.

item.title: Decoding What iOS Location Services Send to Apple: An LLM Is an Unreliable Analyst but a Useful Toolmaker
item.description: Reverse engineering the data formats used by mobile software is skilled and slow, and using AI to assist with it is attractive. We evaluate this for the protobuf messages that an iPhone sends to Apple's location services. Working from Apple's binaries, we use two frontier models (Claude Opus 4.8, Codex GPT Sol 5.6) to reconstruct the schemas of protobufs observed in network traffic. The great majority of the schemas contain substantial errors, and these are hard to detect because the schemas are internally consistent. Direct AI use is therefore unsuitable for forensic and privacy analysis. AI can, however, write reliable analysis tools when their output can be validated. We use Claude to write a Python tool, Extractor, that reliably recovers protobuf schemas from Apple binaries. We validate it against binaries compiled from schemas with known answers, previously published schemas, and network measurements. We demonstrate the use of Extractor to decode and analyse the location services network traffic of a jailbroken iPhone 8 (iOS 16.7.11).

item.title: An Experimental Study on the Functional Correctness of Network Device Configurations Produced by Large Language Models
item.description: This paper presents a preliminary study on the efficacy of network device configuration produced by Large Language Models (LLMs). Currently, the study focuses on routing protocol configurations in a predefined small internetwork with Cisco-based routing devices. The capability of three freely available LLMs with standard capabilities (i.e., with no enhanced features) to produce effective setups is investigated. Prompt engineering methods are excluded in order to assess the "first-response" configurations of the models under consideration. The assessment method is based on the contents of the resulting routing table, aiming at measuring the device functional correctness. For that purpose, the Jaccard index is used to indicate the percentage of correct network prefixes contained in the routing table constructed by the model-based configuration commands. The work provides insights on the maturity and limitations of modern LLMs on aiding network administrators with network device configurations in real deployments.

item.title: Post-Quantum Session Establishment for Matter over Thread: Message Size, Transport, and Protocol Options
item.description: Matter's first post-quantum change protects device attestation with ML-DSA, but its operational handshake, CASE, still derives session keys from P-256 ECDH, so recorded traffic can be decrypted once a quantum computer exists. We quantify the cost of moving CASE to ML-KEM and post-quantum signatures over Thread, where frames carry at most 127 bytes and a Matter message at most 1178 bytes. A byte-exact model of the CASE messages shows that a drop-in ML-KEM-768/ML-DSA-44 handshake grows from 1.6 kB to 22.8 kB and that no fully post-quantum configuration built from FIPS 203/204/205 algorithms fits the message limit. A Monte Carlo model of multi-hop Thread, calibrated to OpenThread and Matter source constants, shows that sending these messages as fragmented IPv6 datagrams causes spurious retransmissions whenever a message and its reply outlast Matter's retransmission timer. At three to four hops the drop-in handshake then takes 1.8 to 2.6 times longer than with a selective-repeat block transfer, with or without interference, and up to 33% of handshakes with sleepy devices fail; raising the timers does not remove the effect. Caching certificate chains and authenticating the device with a pre-distributed ML-KEM key reduce the handshake to 6.1 kB and 44 ms of device computation. As a first step, hybrid P-256+ML-KEM-512 key exchange with a cached device chain protects session keys against harvest-now, decrypt-later attacks while every message still fits the current limit.

item.title: An Experimental Evaluation of Scheduled Transmission and Hardware Timestamping on the Intel E830 NIC
item.description: High-precision packet transmission is increasingly important in deterministic networking applications, including 5G fronthaul and Time-Sensitive Networking (TSN). Some recent high-speed network interface cards (NICs), including the Intel E830 and NVIDIA ConnectX series, support hardware-assisted transmission at specified times and hardware timestamping of received and transmitted frames. Despite the relevance of these capabilities to the stringent timing requirements of 5G fronthaul, little public information is available on their timing accuracy and performance characteristics. As a companion to our previous study of scheduled transmission on the NVIDIA ConnectX series, this paper experimentally characterizes the scheduled transmission and hardware timestamping capabilities of the Intel E830 NIC. Using an FPGA-based measurement platform with deterministic frame generation and nanosecond-resolution timestamping, we evaluate receive and transmit hardware timestamping and scheduled-transmission accuracy. The results show only several-nanosecond timing variation in hardware timestamping. Receive timestamp-derived frame intervals showed a peak-to-peak variation of up to 6 ns, while the transmit timestamp comparison showed a residual range of 4.6 ns after clock-drift compensation. Approximately 99% of the observed frame intervals were within $\pm$300 ns of the target interval, with occasional outliers of up to approximately 2 us. These results indicate that scheduled transmission can support applications with timing requirements on the order of several tens of microseconds, such as 5G fronthaul, but may be insufficient for TSN applications requiring transmission timing accuracy on the order of a few to a few tens of nanoseconds.

item.title: From Echoes to Evidence: Cooperative Fusion for Integrated Sensing and Communication
item.description: Cooperative integrated sensing and communication (ISAC) can support shared situational awareness for unmanned aerial vehicles (UAVs), road vehicles, and industrial mobile robots such as automated guided vehicles (AGVs). Yet multipath can make nodes agree on a virtual target while useful weak echoes remain unexploited. This paper develops cooperative fusion that separates association confirmation, state refinement, and residual recovery. A cellular reference signal model accommodates arbitrary node counts, three-dimensional motion, monostatic and bistatic links, nuisance parameters, and correlated errors. We characterize report distinguishability under bounded bias and shared-reflector ambiguities that survive additional nodes. Minimax estimation yields directional weak-report refinement that preserves confirmed associations and limits bias-sensitive innovations; acquisition accounts for request and upload costs. Controlled experiments accompany UAV evaluations under a Third Generation Partnership Project (3GPP) stochastic channel model and a ray tracing environment representing San Francisco. In the latter environment, matched-budget fusion raises detection from observable site selection's 88.75% to 92.46% and reduces the false-output fraction from 11.06% to 0.40%. Against the strongest full-band fixed site, the 90th-percentile position error on commonly detected targets falls from 8.54 to 3.50 m. Association controls, local rejection ablations, and refinement studies distinguish the sources of these gains.

item.title: When Weak Reports Matter: Staged Anchored Fusion for Cooperative UAV Sensing
item.description: Local multipath rejection can erase evidence needed for cooperative sensing. We propose staged anchored recovery: preserve strong-only confirmations, then query compatible weak reports using unused strong anchors. For any number of sensing nodes, we prove lossless residual screening and derive corroboration and bidirectional cost laws. In 1,024 five-UAV drops, recovery adds 30 matched targets and three false outputs over strict consensus, matching one-pass anchored confirmation's detection counts while reducing weak uploads by 97.4%. Equal-sized cue/report records yield 4.5% less payload than uploading all eligible reports. Independent validation recovers four additional targets with no observed false outputs.

item.title: Evaluating Behavioral Context for Interpretable IAM Policy Risk Scoring in Cloud Environments
item.description: IAM policy analysis typically emphasizes the authorization capabilities encoded in a policy, but security analyst review priority may also depend on the behavioral and environmental context surrounding a policy event. This paper evaluates whether contextual information provides measurable incremental value for interpretable IAM policy risk prioritization beyond policy and effective-authorization information. AWS is used as the experimental cloud provider because its IAM and audit-telemetry ecosystem enables controlled evaluation using AWS IAM Context Bench, a benchmark containing 534 real AWS experimental observations across policy, environment, and behavioral scenarios, including matched cases where policy and environment remain fixed while behavioral context changes. Three Explainable Boosting Machine models are evaluated under the same leakage-controlled grouped cross-validation protocol: a policy-centric baseline, a policy-plus-environment model, and a full-context model incorporating CloudTrail telemetry. The full-context model substantially reduces analyst-priority prediction error relative to the policy-centric baseline and closely tracks the reference priority ordering. In matched same-policy context pairs, the policy-centric model remains invariant, whereas the full-context model separates benign and suspicious behavioral conditions with high directional accuracy. The results also show improved concentration of high-priority cases at the top of simulated analyst review queues. These findings indicate that behavioral and environmental context can provide useful incremental information for analyst-oriented IAM risk prioritization while preserving an interpretable additive model structure. The formulation is applicable beyond AWS conceptually, although cross-provider validation remains future work.

item.title: Poor Privacy Practices Of The Apple App Store: Cookies, Advertising and Tracking Of Users
item.description: We analyse the data that the Apple App Store sends to and receives from Apple servers. We find that multiple cookies are sent by Apple servers and stored on the handset. Adverts with tracking identifiers are also stored on the handset, and we observe that adverts are selected by Apple servers using GDPR special category personal data such as sexuality, religious beliefs and health. User interactions with the Apple App Store (apps and adverts viewed, buttons clicked, searches made etc) are transmitted to Apple servers alongside identifiers linking this data to the individual user and device. We show that much of this data storage and transmission is not essential for the service requested by the user, namely to view, search and install apps. No consent is sought for any of this data storage and processing, and there is no opt out.

item.title: Containing the Autonomous Operator: A Defense-in-Depth Framework and Reference Architecture for Securing AI Agents on Kubernetes
item.description: Large language model (LLM) agents are moving from chat interfaces into infrastructure operations, where they read telemetry, call tools, generate and execute code, and change the state of production Kubernetes clusters. This collapses a boundary that conventional cloud-native security assumes: the boundary between data and control. Content that an agent merely reads (a log line, a ticket, a tool description) can redirect what it does. This paper argues that the model must not be treated as a security boundary and that agent safety on Kubernetes is therefore an infrastructure problem: every guarantee must continue to hold under the assumption that the agent is fully compromised by prompt injection. We contribute (i) a threat model and ten-class threat taxonomy for agents operating on and within Kubernetes, aligned with emerging OWASP guidance for agentic applications; (ii) nine design principles, centered on complete mediation at the tool boundary and on breaking the combination of untrusted input, sensitive access, and external egress; (iii) a seven-layer defense-in-depth framework that maps each principle to native or widely adopted Kubernetes mechanisms: workload identity, RBAC and ValidatingAdmissionPolicy, gVisor/Kata sandboxing via the SIG Apps Agent Sandbox project, FQDN-aware egress policy, an agent/MCP gateway with policy-as-code over tool arguments, and eBPF runtime enforcement; (iv) a reference architecture with concrete policy artifacts and per-layer bindings for Amazon EKS, Azure Kubernetes Service, and Google Kubernetes Engine; and (v) a qualitative evaluation comprising a threat-control coverage matrix and four attack walkthroughs, with a proposed empirical methodology. We report no measured attack-success or overhead figures; instead we identify residual risks and the measurements needed to validate the framework.

item.title: From Alert Floods to Precedence Forests: Zero-Prior-Knowledge Incident Triage with LOGOS
item.description: Commercial observability platforms rely on domain artifacts like distributed traces, topology maps, and baseline metrics. However, when troubleshooting proprietary software, enterprise operators are left with only raw, unannotated text logs. We explore the extreme boundary of log-only diagnosis: To what extent can we isolate failure propagation using strictly raw text logs? We present LOGOS, an unsupervised system that exploits entity-event co-occurrence and temporal precedence to collapse millions of raw log lines into a compact precedence forest. Evaluated across 25 production enterprise outages and 12 open-source issues, LOGOS operates with zero prior knowledge---requiring no seed queries, observed symptoms, or pre-defined incident boundaries. In a median wall-time of 4.5 minutes, LOGOS eliminates a median 99.8% of background noise, achieves 0.76 mean recall, and detects failure cascades with a 16-hour median diagnosis-verified lead time---consolidating alert floods 124x to enable 80% enterprise (100% open-source) zero-shot LLM root-cause accuracy.

item.title: Line-Rate GTP-U Admission Control at the Edge of a Cloud-Native 5G Core: An XDP-Based Design for Kubernetes-Hosted User Plane Functions
item.description: The User Plane Function (UPF) of a 5G Standalone core terminates every GPRS Tunnelling Protocol user-plane (GTP-U) packet arriving from the radio access network, which makes its N3 interface both the busiest and the most exposed point of the mobile data path. As operators migrate the core onto Kubernetes and public cloud, the UPF increasingly shares a general-purpose Linux kernel with other workloads, and kernel-bypass frameworks such as DPDK become harder to operate. This paper presents GTP-Guard, a design for line-rate GTP-U admission control built on the eXpress Data Path (XDP) hook of the Linux kernel. GTP-Guard drops illegitimate tunnel traffic in the network driver, before socket-buffer allocation, using six ordered stages: peer allow-listing, GTP-U header validation, Tunnel Endpoint Identifier (TEID) admission against session state derived from the Packet Forwarding Control Protocol (PFCP), bounded extension-header parsing, inner-packet anti-spoofing with GTP-in-GTP detection, and per-session policing. We formalize stage ordering as a cost-minimization problem and show that sorting stages by the ratio of per-packet cost to rejection probability minimizes expected per-packet work, which motivates run-time reordering through tail-call program arrays when traffic mix shifts under attack. We further describe a Kubernetes deployment model based on a node-level DaemonSet with pinned eBPF maps that survive agent upgrades, discuss constraints specific to public-cloud virtual NICs, and define a reproducible evaluation methodology, with explicit hypotheses, for throughput, latency, CPU efficiency and attack resilience. This paper presents the design and methodology; experimental results will be reported in a subsequent version.

item.title: Characterizing the eBPF-Based Data Plane for Multi-ClusterKubernetes: A Systematic Evaluation of Cilium Cluster Meshand KVStoreMesh
item.description: Kubernetes deployments increasingly span multiple clusters for reasons of scale, fault isolation, regulatory boundaries, and heterogeneous hardware placement, including GPU-dense clusters dedicated to AI and HPC workloads. Cilium Cluster Mesh, built on extended Berkeley Packet Filter (eBPF) technology, has emerged as a widely deployed mechanism for connecting such clusters into a single logical network without a dedicated multi-cluster gateway. Despite its adoption, the academic literature contains no systematic, reproducible evaluation of the eBPF-based multi-cluster data plane itself: existing work either benchmarks eBPF against iptables within a single cluster, or applies eBPF to cross-cluster monitoring rather than forwarding and identity propagation. The most detailed scale data available - a report of a clustermesh-apiserver failing under load at approximately 45,000 nodes across 256 clusters - comes from an industry engineering blog rather than a peer-reviewed source. This paper proposes a methodology to close that gap. We define five research questions covering latency, throughput, control-plane limits, churn, and GPU/RDMA sensitivity, and describe a testbed and eBPF-level instrumentation design. Lacking a live multi-cluster testbed for this submission, we report results from a calibrated analytical simulation of control-plane architectures fit to the production data point. These results are presented as falsifiable predictions intended for validation once the testbed is complete. This paper provides the motivation, experimental design, and preliminary simulation results to serve as a template for a full empirical study.

item.title: Configuration-Induced Delivery Failures in NATS JetStream: Detection and Remediation
item.description: NATS JetStream's at-least-once delivery guarantee is conditional: five common configuration mistakes silently violate it, causing duplicate message processing, data loss, or redelivery storms with no error logged anywhere. The standard Prometheus NATS exporter exposes only server-level throughput metrics and cannot detect any of these failures. We present nats-lens, a standalone monitor that reads from the JetStream management API and detects all five violation classes without requiring changes to monitored applications or client code. We formally characterize each class with a precise condition, prove that standard Prometheus NATS metrics are structurally incapable of detecting any of them, and implement five targeted detectors. In a controlled evaluation of 30 rounds per scenario on both single-node and 3-node JetStream clusters, nats-lens achieves 100% detection coverage across all five classes---versus 0% for the baseline---with zero false positives over 30 minutes of healthy operation. Detection latency ranges from 2,003 ms to 8,013 ms (within three poll cycles). We confirm language-agnostic detection empirically using consumers in Rust, Go, and Python. The tool is open source and exposes findings through four output channels: web dashboard, Prometheus metrics, REST API, and NATS health events.

item.title: Unknown-Traffic Detection, Calibration and Shortcut Reliance in Distilled Encrypted-Traffic Classifiers over One Year
item.description: Knowledge distillation is the standard way to compress encrypted-traffic classifiers for the edge, and almost all such work judges students by accuracy alone. We ask what else a student inherits: unknown-traffic detection, calibration, shortcut reliance, and whether any survives a year of drift. Resemblance proves little on its own, since soft targets also regularise. We therefore distil one 101k-parameter student from two teachers of equal accuracy but different construction, a five-member ensemble and a single wider model, so that following one rather than the other is attributable to it. The design was pre-registered before any test result was seen. We tested ten hypotheses on CESNET-TLS-Year22, a year of real TLS traffic, across 18 test windows over 35 weeks. Two are supported: a student's per-flow unknown-scores shift toward its own teacher, but only at a conventional temperature, not the accuracy-optimal one; and a shortcut-reliant teacher passes its over-confidence to a student that never sees the feature. The drift prediction is reversed under both scores, the gap narrowing rather than widening and the student overtaking under the energy score in two of three replicates, as is the prediction that such a teacher harms its student's detection, which improves slightly. Shortcut reliance is set by model size, not distillation. Under the logit-based scores nothing else transfers: distillation beats neither a temperature-scaled direct student nor label smoothing. Exploratory analysis shows this turns on the scoring rule: with a feature-space detector the teacher detects unknown traffic 0.073 AUROC better than the direct student, where the energy score sees 0.000, and the conventional-temperature student inherits most of it. Label smoothing, with no teacher, recovers more. Distillation transfers the teacher's habits; what looks like an inherited ability is available without one.

item.title: Packet iSlip
item.description: This paper examines input/output buffered crossbar switches under combined packet and cell data. Our switch architecture uses input buffering with Virtual Output Queues to avoid Head of Line Blocking. The switch fabric is a crossbar with no speedup. We use a modified iSlip [McKeown] crossbar scheduler geared towards packet data, called piSlip. Cell ports are largely unmodified from standard iSlip behavior. For packet output ports, we introduce changes to the grant pointer which minimizes output latency caused by packet reassembly. Our model uses several output states, including packet cut-through. From simulation results, we show that piSlip with virtual cut-through offers latency characteristics significantly better than unmodified iSlip with similar packet port interfaces. Simulation further shows that piSlip and iSlip have similar maximum and average buffering requirements.

item.title: Joint Effects of Node Density, Propagation, Wi-Fi Generation, and Transport Protocol on WLAN Performance: An ns-3 Study
item.description: Wireless local area network (WLAN) performance is jointly shaped by medium contention, propagation, Wi-Fi configuration, and transport-layer behavior. This study evaluates IEEE 802.11g and IEEE 802.11ax in a single-access-point uplink topology, comparing UDP and TCP under Friis, LogDistance, and cascaded Friis-Nakagami propagation models. The factorial design spans 5 to 50 stations, six access-point distances from 5 m to 50 m, and three random seeds. Of 1,080 scheduled executions, 1,073 produced valid CSV outputs; seven runs terminated with internal ns-3 and cppyy segmentation errors and were excluded. Across the global scenario summaries, TCP FlowMonitor packet delivery ratios (PDRs) range from 0.994 to 0.997, whereas UDP PDRs range from 0.298 to 0.731. The highest mean aggregate throughput is 2.619 Mb/s for TCP under the configured IEEE 802.11ax mode with Friis propagation; UDP reaches 25.854 Mb/s in the same topology. These results show that packet delivery ratio, throughput, delay, and fairness must be considered together. FlowMonitor metrics are IP-flow observations, so the study does not establish application-level delivery or isolate optional IEEE 802.11ax multi-user mechanisms.

item.title: Learning to Maximize Energy Efficiency in 6G in-X Subnetworks
item.description: This paper investigates energy-efficient power control in 6G in-X subnetworks. We consider a graph neural network (GNN) framework that captures inter-subnetwork interference and the underlying wireless topology to optimize transmit powers. Three energy efficiency (EE) formulations are studied: (i) network-centric, which maximizes total network energy efficiency; (ii) subnetwork-centric, which maximizes the average energy efficiency per subnetwork; and (iii) a multi-objective approach, which balances energy efficiency and sum-rate performance. Extensive simulations in industrial factory settings with 3GPP channel models demonstrate that the GNN effectively learns interference-aware power allocation policies, significantly outperforming maximum power transmission and existing GNN based power control solution. Results showed network EE gains of up to 1341%, average per-device EE improvements of up to 1302%, and sum-rate enhancements up to 24.7% relative to a maximum transmit power policy, depending on the chosen optimization formulation and trade-off settings.

item.title: Explanation-Guided Federated Deep Reinforcement Learning for Joint Resource Allocation and Scheduling in 6G in-X Subnetworks
item.description: Sixth-generation (6G) wireless systems are envisioned as networks of networks, integrating diverse in-X subnetworks that provide localized, high-performance connectivity. Ensuring reliable communication in dense deployments, such as industrial robots and vehicles, is challenging due to dynamic interference and strict performance requirements. Traditional radio resource management (RRM) methods have limitations, prompting the need for AI-based solutions. In this paper, we address the challenges of dynamic resource allocation and scheduling in 6G in-X subnetworks supporting applications with heterogeneous characteristics by proposing a novel framework that combines Multi-Agent Reinforcement Learning (MARL), Federated Learning (FL), and Explainable AI (XAI). Our solution is designed to improve the reliability, robustness, and transparency of resource management and intra-subnetwork scheduling while ensuring data privacy and fairness across multiple co-existing subnetworks. Unlike existing works, our approach considers a realistic scenario with multiple devices per subnetwork, thereby offering a more comprehensive and scalable solution. The proposed explainable RL framework enables agents to collaboratively optimize channel allocation and scheduling without the need to share raw data, preserving the privacy of each participating subnetwork. Extensive simulations based on 3GPP scenarios demonstrate the effectiveness of our approach, showing significant improvements in performance, and transparency over existing solutions.

item.title: Remote IoT Source Monitoring with Delayed Feedback
item.description: Remote source monitoring is a key use case for Internet of things (IoT) applications, calling on efficient communications protocols to ensure timely data delivery. In this paper, we consider a practically inspired scenario in which an IoT device reports sensor readings to a gateway over a correlated, lossy channel, receiving feedback on the transmission outcome only after some delay. For this setting, we investigate practical threshold-based reporting strategies for monitoring a Markov process, and evaluate two approaches: a reactive strategy where the node awaits feedback after an update, and a proactive strategy that preemptively transmits a second update. Leveraging Markov renewal processes, we provide an exact performance analysis in terms of the mean squared error (MSE). Our study characterizes the fundamental trade-off between estimation error and communication rate, revealing that proactive transmissions significantly improve MSE even under strict IoT rate constraints.

item.title: SMS-delivered network-initiated SUPL on Pixel 8: a privacy assessment
item.description: A SUPL\_INIT message is a network-initiated trigger that can be sent to a handset using an SMS to unilaterally start a location session: on receipt, the handset is instructed to determine its own position and report it, together with an identifier such as its IMSI, to a server specified in the message, without any action by the phone's user. The concern motivating this investigation is whether such a message could be used to silently exfiltrate a handset's location and subscriber identity to a server under an attacker's control. We investigated this on a Google Pixel 8 handset, which uses a Samsung Exynos modem and a Broadcom GPS/GNSS subsystem. We find no privacy issue: the handset never sends location data to an attacker-chosen server as a result of an unsolicited SUPL\_INIT delivered by SMS.

item.title: Provisional Reachability: Containing Agents by Making Every Crossing Revocable
item.description: A companion paper found that what a defender must block over time has units: bits per period [Takashita, 2026a]. This paper sets it. Hold every crossing in escrow for one period, audit each held item independently with probability r, and revoke the window if any audit catches something. An adversary crossing k times, each carrying c bits, expects kc(1-r)^k, maximised at k* = 1/ln(1/(1-r)), a bound of L(r) ~ c/(er) per window. The bound is a supremum over the adversary's choice, so the scheme may be public; simulation matches it to 7.7 standard errors. It is a rate, not a total: escrow alone still lets the secret assemble in every run. But if the secret decays at a fraction mu of held bits per period, holdings converge to g/mu at any horizon, so an L-bit secret is unreachable once mu > g/L -- an error threshold in Eigen's sense, sharp where the closed form puts it (100% of runs assemble at 0.9mu*, 0% at 2mu*, over 20,000 windows). Deception that needs the adversary to reason badly fails: a surface whose names lie left accuracy at 18 of 18, and 100% at three reader strengths. Withholding reference works, and differently: no reader would commit at all. Keying the entry points hides 0.10 bits of what a module does; keying the denotation hides 2.64 of 3.00 at chance accuracy, while 100% of readers still call it ordinary Python. Variance must be removed from the audit rate, where loot is convex in r, and added to the activation budget, where survival is multiplicative: extinction 70% to 100% at a fixed mean. End to end the stack takes the leak from 100,000 to 59 bits, a factor of 1,704, leaving 12% of legitimate work standing; keying the window to the caller restores that to 100% at no cost in leakage, at the price of a bound that is per principal. Of 65 read-only tools, escrow leaves 2,400 bits per call: a factor of 10, not infinity.

item.title: Reachability, Not Observation: Containing Systems Whose Wiring Changes
item.description: Containment decisions -- where to put a firewall, which links to monitor, what a program may reach -- are computed from an observed structure, and observation is a snapshot. We ask what a snapshot misses when the wiring changes over time. On a hypercube whose active dimension rotates, a balanced split shows zero crossing edges at 93% of instants, yet 8,192 edges must be blocked permanently; adding one always-on ring, a defender sees 2 where 8,194 must be blocked, a factor of 4,097. A time-aware defender holds 585 blocks on average, but one step of clock lag drops its containment to 0%. On the real Internet the same gap is only x1.8-2.0 (1997-2000) and x1.5-1.6 (2024-2026) once growth is removed, so the blind spot is introduced by design, not inherited from the world -- and it has been designed: the round-robin schedules of optical datacentre fabrics have a gap equal to their period. A declared capability map, checked by static reachability over a real application's call graph, catches all 8 planted holes; the string deny-list previously in place catches 2. One calculation generates every number from one parameter, the period, and reads three boundaries not usually called schedules: frequency hopping, whose standard results are these closed forms with channels in place of edges; the air gap, whose always-on crossing set is empty and whose known breach came at the one phase a snapshot misses; and the tool surface of a coding agent, inventoried from the inside. Turning the cuts on that agent: idle, its instantaneous state cut is zero, while 6 channels carry it across a context reset, none of them the network, so severing the network removes 0. The channel that spawns copies is a branching process with a sharp threshold at approval rate 1/b, below which denial is unnecessary and above which denial is insufficient. Contain by the paths that exist, not by the behaviour that was seen.

item.title: ABDS: Classifying Protocol Divergence Causes via AS-Boundary Correlation
item.description: Network operators frequently encounter protocol divergence---where ICMP, TCP, and UDP experience different treatment along a path. Existing tools identify where divergence occurs but not why, forcing manual investigation that delays resolution. We present two contributions: (1) the AS-Boundary Divergence Score (ABDS), a metric that correlates protocol divergence locations with BGP topology to automatically classify causes as routing-policy-driven versus internal-policy-driven; and (2) the localhost response signature, an empirical finding that security appliances return 127.0.0.1 in TTL-exceeded messages to mask their IPs. We evaluate ABDS against 496 targets across 8 categories (Finance, Government, Education, Healthcare, Tech, E-commerce, Media, International), with multi-vantage validation from 10+ global locations confirming routing consistency. ABDS achieves 100% classification accuracy on verified divergent targets (50/50), significantly outperforming majority-class baseline (54%, McNemar's p < 0.001). The localhost signature achieves 100% precision (18/18, 95% CI: [82%, 100%]) in identifying security appliances across 9 categories including government (IRS, USPS, VA), finance, and healthcare. Our open-source Rust implementation enables automated escalation decisions, reducing mean-time-to-resolution for network operators.

item.title: Toward a Layer-2 Trigger for AI/ML Lifecycle Management in 6G
item.description: 3GPP has progressively expanded AI/ML lifecycle management in the radio access network, from one-sided model control to Release 20 support for two-sided CSI-feedback model pairing. Yet a basic control question remains: when monitoring detects degradation, how quickly must a corrective action take effect? To expose this dependency, we stress-test three activation and rollback strategies in a surrogate regime-shift environment using 150 independently trained PPO candidate policies, each evaluated over 20 matched noise realizations. We add 0-40 control-step delay only to corrective lifecycle commands. With no added delay, stability-gated blending reduces mean post-shift cumulative SLA deficit from 47.02 to 7.57 violation-steps relative to hard cutover; at 40 steps, the deficit rises to 44.38, only 5.6% below the hard-cutover baseline. KPI-threshold rollback loses its advantage within only a few control intervals, while blending degrades more gradually. These results do not set a physical 6G latency bound. They show why timing requirements matter for corrective actions: lifecycle performance depends on when the command takes effect. Motivated by Layer-1/Layer-2 Triggered Mobility, we examine a standards split in which Layer 3 retains lifecycle configuration while a compact Layer 2 trigger is considered only for the latency-critical subset, together with pair-consistency, local-fallback, and security/freshness requirements.

item.title: terms.txt: A Consent and Compensation Protocol for Agentic Web Access
item.description: The open web ran on an unwritten bargain: sites admitted crawlers, and search engines sent visitors back. Public measurements show that bargain breaking under AI crawlers and agents. Automated clients now make up most requests, training dominates Cloudflare-classified crawling, and the largest AI platforms fetch thousands of pages for each visitor they return. The web's common control, robots.txt, cannot express identity, purpose, terms, or price, can be circumvented, and newer alternatives are largely proprietary CDN features. We specify terms.txt, a robots.txt-style file for per-path, per-purpose machine-access terms, plus an origin-enforced exchange using Web Bot Auth signatures, signed intent, delegation tokens, HTTP 402 negotiation, and signed receipts. We define what the exchange can enforce, audit, and leave to contract. A dependency-free implementation adds 0.20 to 0.65 ms per request on one vCPU.

item.title: Hybrid Continuous DoA Estimation with Shared-Radius Co-Prime Circular Arrays
item.description: This paper proposes a shared-radius co-prime circular array for high-resolution, continuous 2D Direction-of-Arrival (DoA) estimation in 3D space, jointly estimating azimuth and elevation angles. The proposed architecture consists of two uniform circular sub-arrays with co-prime antenna counts sharing a common radius RR, a design that intrinsically suppresses mutual coupling leakage compared to dense uniform arrays. Unlike existing works that rely on complex phase-mode transformations to map circular structures to virtual linear arrays, we introduce a hybrid continuous-recovery framework operating directly in the physical spatial domain. By integrating a fast, discrete coarse-grid search with a swarm-intelligence continuous refinement stage, the proposed method completely bypasses discrete grid-mismatch limitations and computationally expensive eigenvalue decompositions. A rigorous theoretical analysis using Nivens Theorem establishes the spatial uniqueness of the true source direction, effectively resolving phase ambiguities. Simulation results demonstrate that this hybrid scheme achieves superior resolution and lower Root Mean Square Error (RMSE) at low Signal-to-Noise Ratios (SNR) compared to uniform configurations, while asymptotically converging to the theoretical Cramer-Rao Bound (CRB) at high SNRs.

item.title: Det-5G: Closing the Determinism Gap in 5G-Advanced for Industrial Closed-Loop Control
item.description: The ultra-reliable low-latency communication (uRLLC) capability of 5G has created significant opportunities for industrial wireless connectivity, yet widespread use of cellular networks for closed-loop control remains challenging. Closed-loop control requires more than low packet latency and high reliability: cyclic command/feedback exchanges must complete within predictable time bounds despite changing channel conditions, recovery transmissions, mobility, and multi-device contention. This paper introduces Deterministic-5G (Det-5G), a unified radio resource allocation framework for industrial closed-loop control. Det-5G treats the complete bidirectional control cycle as the scheduling object and combines coordinated downlink/uplink allocation, adaptive bundled transmissions, group-oriented downlink communication, and optimized multi-user uplink scheduling over 5G air-interface. Its performance is evaluated through a combination of closed-form analysis and Monte Carlo scheduling experiments, with comparisons against conventional dynamic grant-based scheduling, semi-persistent scheduling/configured grant operation, and fixed proactive repetition. The evaluation shows that Det-5G improves predictability of cycle completion, maintains the target reliability under changing link conditions, and scales more effectively to multi-device control than conventional reactive scheduling, while adapting radio resource use instead of continuously provisioning for the worst case as in fixed repetition. These characteristics make cycle-oriented scheduling a pragmatic solution for reducing the determinism gap that limits the use of 5G for closed-loop control in different verticals, especially as it evolves through 5G-Advanced toward 6G.

item.title: The LQ Digital Mode Family: Protocol Architecture and Reference Specification for Weak-Signal Communications
item.description: This paper introduces LQ8, an open-source weak-signal digital mode for amateur radio that completes structured two-way contacts in 4 transmissions (60 s), achieving a 1.50x speedup over canonical 6-transmission exchanges (90 s) and 1.25x over 5-transmission RR73 exchanges (75 s) while preserving complete bidirectional exchange of Maidenhead grid locators, signal reports, and mutual acknowledgments. By replacing fixed-width message-type headers with variable-length prefix codes matched to physical-layer bit budgets, LQ8 packs the answering station's grid locator and measured signal report into a single 77-bit reply. In multi-station pileup operations, LQ8 confirms up to two answering stations simultaneously within a single-carrier, constant-envelope 50.0 Hz transmission with a 0.0 dB RF power-splitting penalty, enabling a theoretical peak rate of up to 160 QSOs/h (scaling to 320 QSOs/h in dual-carrier operation) while retaining the -21.0 dB SNR sensitivity of continuous-phase 8-GFSK transport. The protocol family also defines three extended profiles (LQ16, LQ4, and LQ2) tailored for extreme sensitivity, VHF/UHF contesting, and fast-burst channels.

item.title: SLA-Safe Energy Control for AI-Native NG-RAN Using Stability-Aware Constrained PPO
item.description: One important AI-for-RAN use case is energy saving, in which radio resources and cell energy modes must be dynamically controlled without violating user quality-of-service (QoS) or service-level agreement (SLA) requirements. However, aggressive sleep-state or deactivation decisions may reduce energy consumption at the cost of throughput degradation, delay increase, SLA violations, and unstable mode switching, especially under time-varying and bursty traffic conditions. This paper proposes a stability-aware constrained reinforcement learning framework for SLA-safe energy control in 5G NG-RAN. The problem is formulated as a constrained Markov decision process in which an AI-native controller selects closed-loop energy-saving actions based on cell load, queue status, active-user information, current energy mode, and SLA-related indicators. The proposed framework uses constrained proximal policy optimization with adaptive Lagrangian penalties to account for throughput, delay, and SLA constraints. To improve operation under traffic distribution shift, the controller is trained using mixed nominal and stress traffic regimes, while a switching-stability penalty is introduced to reduce oscillatory transitions between active and low-power modes. Simulation results in a seven-cell NG-RAN environment show that the proposed controller reduces energy consumption by approximately 41.4% under nominal traffic, 10.5% under stress traffic, and 22.9% under unseen-stress traffic relative to the Always-On baseline. Under stress and unseen-stress traffic, the controller preserves zero SLA violation and zero throughput loss, indicating service-preserving operation under challenging conditions. The proposed method also reduces switching activity compared with basic threshold-based energy saving.

item.title: Will there be a 7G?
item.description: The transition from 5G to 6G is becoming concrete: the ITU-R IMT-2030 framework has established the high-level vision and capability set for 6G, while 3GPP Release 21 has defined the path toward the first 6G specifications. This raises a deliberately provocative question for the research and standards communities: will there be a 7G, and if so, what would justify it? This paper argues that 7G should not be treated as an inevitable numbering exercise or as a catalogue of more ambitious radio targets. Instead, its justification should depend on whether post-6G systems introduce needs or coordination problems that cannot be met by 6G/6G-Advanced, Wi-Fi, NTN, private cellular, neutral-host deployments, edge-cloud platforms, or complementary wireless and software-based systems. To support this assessment, the paper develops a readiness framework covering demand-led need, system-level discontinuity, coordination value, sustainability and circularity, trust, and geopolitical viability. It then applies the framework to candidate 7G discontinuities, including agentic network operation, RF-native computing, quantum-enabled interworking, policy-aware spectrum governance, grid-interactive infrastructure, outcome-assured services, and regionalized standards. The contribution is not a prediction of a fixed 7G architecture, but a structured basis for deciding whether 7G should become a distinct mobile generation, an extension of 6G evolution, or a broader post-6G infrastructure fabric.

item.title: Real-Time Neuromorphic Spectrum Intelligence Simulator
